sbh4.1:8.4: They are in turn bases for pleasant feeling, bases for painful feeling, or bases for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
sbh4.1:8.5: The bases for pleasant feeling are bound to *kāma-rāga*,
sbh4.1:8.7: The bases for painful feeling are bound to hatred, anger, resentment.
sbh4.1:8.8: The bases for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are bound to concealment, malice, deception, fraud, shamelessness, lack of remorse, and view-perversion.
sbh4.1:8.9: Thus these sense-pleasures are followed by tainted feelings and by their corresponding defilements.' Thus he investigates the specific characteristic of sense-pleasures.
sbh4.1:9.1: How does he investigate the general characteristic?
sbh4.1:9.2: 'All these sense-pleasures, together with the suffering-of-birth, the suffering-of-aging, up through the suffering-of-thwarted-desire, are equally bound and bound-together.
sbh4.1:9.3: Even those sense-pleasure-enjoyers who proceed in great sense-pleasure-abundance —
sbh4.1:9.4: they too are not free from the *dharmatā* of birth-and-the-rest. Their abundance is only momentary.'
sbh4.1:9.5: Thus he investigates the general characteristic.
sbh4.1:10.1: How does he investigate the side?
sbh4.1:10.2: 'These sense-pleasures fall on the dark side.
sbh4.1:10.3: They are like a skeleton, like a piece of meat, like a grass-torch;
sbh4.1:10.10: experience the suffering of the seeking.
sbh4.1:10.11: They experience the suffering of guarding, of loss-of-affection, of dissatisfaction, of non-autonomy, of misconduct.
sbh4.1:10.12: So also for one indulging in sense-pleasures.
sbh4.1:10.13: Five faults have been spoken of
sbh4.1:10.14: by the Blessed One: 'Sense-pleasures give little gratification, much suffering, much fault.'
sbh4.1:10.15: 'To one indulging in sense-pleasures, there is no measure of satisfaction or sufficiency. By this enumeration, sense-pleasures are reproached by the Buddhas, by the Buddha-disciples, by the well-gone ones, by the noble persons.'
sbh4.1:10.16: 'To one indulging in sense-pleasures, the fetters go to accumulation.'
sbh4.1:10.17: 'There is no evil, unwholesome action that I say is not-to-be-done [by such a one].'
sbh4.1:10.18: 'These sense-pleasures are dissatisfaction-makers, common, causes of unrighteous and unequal conduct;
sbh4.1:10.19: increasers of sense-craving, to be avoided by the noble, swift-going to sense-objects, dependent on conditions, places of heedlessness, hollow, impermanent, vain, falsely-pretending, illusion-like, child-prattle.'
sbh4.1:10.20: Whether sense-pleasures of this very life,
sbh4.1:10.21: or of the next life, whether divine or human —
sbh4.1:10.22: beginning with Māra, this is Māra's range, this is Māra's pasture, where these manifold evil, unwholesome mental dharmas come about:
sbh4.1:10.23: namely covetousness, ill-will, agitation — or whatever else is obstructive to a noble disciple in training. By many enumerations these sense-pleasures fall on the dark side.
sbh4.1:10.24: By this much, in this manner, he investigates the side.
sbh4.1:11.1: 'Across past, future, and present times — these sense-pleasures are impermanent in every time, unstable in every time.
sbh4.1:11.2: Thus they are with-many-troubles, with-many-afflictions, with-many-faults.' Thus he investigates time.
sbh4.1:12.2: 'With great endeavor, with great seeking, with great labor, by various assorted craftsmanship-and-occupations, sense-pleasures are gathered.
sbh4.1:12.4: Once gathered well and generated well,
sbh4.1:12.5: they extend as far as external objects of attachment: mother, father, son, wife, female slave, male slave, worker, servant, friend, minister, kinsman, blood-relation.
sbh4.1:12.6: Or, with respect to this inward body — of form, gross, made of the four great elements, accumulated by gruel and barley, subject to constant smearing, washing, rubbing, breaking, cutting, scattering, and destruction — they serve merely as counteractions to sufferings as they arise.
sbh4.1:12.7: Food is the counter-action of the suffering of hunger.
sbh4.1:12.8: Clothing is the counter-action of the suffering of cold and heat,
sbh4.1:12.10: Bedding is the counter-action of the suffering of sleep-fatigue.
sbh4.1:12.11: Walking-and-standing is the counter-action of the suffering of posture.
sbh4.1:12.12: And for the counter-action of the suffering of illness,
sbh4.1:12.13: medicine for the sick — these sense-pleasures are counteractions to suffering.'
sbh4.1:12.14: 'These are not to be enjoyed with attachment,
sbh4.1:12.15: nor with clinging — except by one ill, weakened, suffering, taking medicine simply for the appeasement of illness. So this is trustworthy testimony.'
sbh4.1:12.16: 'So these sense-pleasures are gross thus and thus.'
sbh4.1:12.17: 'Direct knowing-and-seeing has also arisen in me.'
sbh4.1:12.19: It is also the nature of sense-pleasures — beginningless, established-dharma, unthinkable-dharma.
sbh4.1:12.20: It is not to be thought.
sbh4.1:12.21: It is not to be discriminated. Thus he investigates reasoning.

sbh4.1:24.14: All [are] past, future, present; arisen from causes, arisen dependently; bodily, momentary;

sbh4.1:24.18: 'Not calm, not very calm' — by such modes the [practitioner] discerns the grossness-mark in vitarkas.
sbh4.1:24.19: The dhyāna [is called calm] from the departure of [the first dhyāna's] grossness.
sbh4.1:24.20: The remaining attentions for the second-dhyāna-attainment are to be known as appropriate, just as [for] yoga, as before.
sbh4.1:24.21: Thus stage by stage, up through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, seven attentions are to be known as appropriate.
